div.p: Background Determining isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) mutation status in glioma is important for determining prognosis. We aimed to compare supervised and semi-supervised machine learning (ML) models in glioma IDH1 mutation status prediction using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-derived radiomics features.

div.head: Methods
div.p: Images and segmentation masks from several public collections, including ACRIN-FMISO, CPTAC-GBM, IvyGAP, TCGA-GBM, TCGA-LGG, UCSF-PDGM, UPENN-GBM, and REMBRANDT, were retrieved from The Cancer Imaging Archive (TCIA) portal. These data were divided into training cohort 1, unlabeled cohort, holdout internal validation (HOIV) cohort, and external validation (EV) cohort. After image preprocessing, radiomics features were extracted from T1-weighted, T1 contrast-enhanced (T1CE), T2-weighted, and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) sequences. The least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (Lasso) algorithm was used for feature selection. Supervised and semi-supervised models were then constructed using 10 ML algorithms and various sequence combinations. For supervised models, we used training cohort 1 to develop the models. Regarding semi-supervised models, we initially predicted the labels of the unlabeled cohort using the training cohort 1 (pseudolabeling), then concatenated the training cohort 1 with these pseudolabeled data to create training cohort 2, and subsequently developed models using the training cohort 2. Both supervised and semi-supervised models were then validated on HOIV and EV cohorts.

Results Data for 436, 151, 110, and 535 patients were included in the training cohort 1, unlabeled cohort, HOIV cohort, and EV cohort, respectively. A semi-supervised model using 24 features from T1CE images yielded the highest AUC on EV (0.951), which was significantly higher than the best supervised model (AUC = 0.917, p = 0.005). The latter model was constructed using 30 features from FLAIR and T1CE sequences. Furthermore, across all sequence combinations, the semi-supervised models consistently achieved higher AUCs in the EV cohort.

div.head: Background
div.p: Gliomas are the most common primary tumors of the central nervous system (CNS) [1].

e World Health Organization 2021 guideline for classification of CNS tumors highlighted the importance of isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) status as a crucial biomarker for glioma classification and prognosis [2]. Gliomas with IDH mutation have a more favorable prognosis compared to wild-type tumors [3]. erefore, determining IDH status in glioma patients is important for guiding personalized treatment and predicting prognosis.

Current routine methods for assessing IDH mutation status depend on invasive tissue sampling, which carries inherent risks including bleeding and neurological complications [4,5]. Moreover, these procedures may not always be feasible in patients with inoperable or anatomically inaccessible tumors, such as those located in deep or eloquent brain regions [5]. ese limitations highlight the need for noninvasive, accurate, and widely accessible techniques for molecular characterization of gliomas.

Radiomics involves the extraction of features from medical images, such as magnetic resonance images (MRIs), which can then be used for diagnostic purposes [6]. Advances in machine learning (ML) model development, along with access to large annotated neuroimaging datasets, have led to the creation of radiomics-based ML models for glioma molecular subtyping [7]. However, most of these models depend solely on supervised learning, which requires a large amount of fully-labeled data, a challenge in clinical practice.

To overcome this limitation, semi-supervised learning methods may be beneficial by utilizing both labeled and unlabeled data to generate pseudolabels, effectively expanding the training dataset [8]. In this approach, samples with available data (e.g., available glioma MRI and known IDH mutation status) are used as a training cohort to predict the labels of an unlabeled cohort (e.g., available glioma MRI and unknown IDH mutation status). is results in the generation of pseudolabels for the unlabeled cohort. ese two cohorts can be then merged to create a new training cohort with a higher sample size and be used for outcome prediction in a validation cohort. is approach may enhance model performance, particularly in situations where labeled data is limited. In this study, we aimed to evaluate and compare the performance of supervised and semi-supervised models using several ML algorithms.

div.head: Datasets and data splitting
div.p: MRIs and segmentation masks of the patients who had preoperative T1-weighted (T1W), T1 contrast-enhanced (T1CE), T2-weighted (T2W), and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) MRI and available masks were retrieved from the RSNA-ASNR-MICCAI-BraTS-2021 dataset [9] using e Cancer Imaging Archive (TCIA) website [10].
is dataset includes images from multiple collections namely ACRIN-FMISO, CPTAC-GBM, IvyGAP, TCGA-GBM, TCGA-LGG, UCSF-PDGM, and UPENN-GBM.

e RSNA-ASNR-MICCAI-BraTS-2021 dataset only contains some of the images from UCSF-PDGM and UPENN-GBM collections. To expand our dataset, we also retrieved non-mutual images for these two collections from TCIA [11,12]. Additionally, images and segmentation masks of the REMBRANDT collection were retrieved [13,14].
is led to an initial cohort of 1329 patients. Detailed imaging protocols are available at TCIA and original publications [10][11][12][15][16][17][18][19][20].

Segmentation masks of the RSNA-ASNR-MICCAI-BraTS-2021 and non-mutual UCSF-PDGM datasets were generated using the STAPLE fusion of the three top-performing BraTS algorithms, including nnU-Net, Deep-Scan, and DeepMedic. e resulting labels were then manually refined by volunteer neuroradiology experts with varying levels of training and experience, and finally approved by one of two board-certified attending neuroradiologists with over 15 years of experience in glioma imaging [9]. Tumors in the non-mutual UPENN-GBM dataset were also segmented using the fused automated model [12]. For the REMBRANDT dataset, tumor segmentation was already performed automatically using GLISTRboost [14].

e datasets we utilized provide three tumor masks including the enhancing tumor, non-enhancing tumor, and peritumoral edema area. To streamline the process, we merged the three subregions and applied a single mask. IDH1 status was determined using immunohistochemical or sequencing methods and was collected from the Genomic Data Commons (GDC) data portal or TCIA. Institutional review board approval and informed consent were not required for this study because all data were obtained from publicly available deidentified datasets.

e retrieved data were divided into a developmentinternal validation cohort (ACRIN-FMISO, CPTAC-GBM, IvyGAP, REMBRANDT, TCGA-GBM, and Conclusion Semi-supervised approaches may improve the performance of radiomics-based ML models in predicting glioma IDH1 status. Using pseudolabels, these models can increase the size of training data, potentially leading to enhancement of model predictive performance. Additionally, these models may improve prediction efficiency by requiring fewer image sequences. Keywords Brain tumor, Molecular subtype, Radiogenomics, Texture analysis UCSF-PDGM) and an initial external validation (EV) cohort (TCGA-LGG and UPENN-GBM). In the development-internal validation cohort, patients without available IDH1 status were regarded as the unlabeled cohort (n = 151) and patients with available IDH1 status were further split into the training cohort 1 (80%, 72 IDH1 mutated and 364 IDH1 wildtype) and the holdout internal validation (HOIV) cohort (20%, n = 32 IDH1 mutated and 78 IDH1 wildtype). Patients with no available IDH1 status in the initial EV cohort were omitted, leading to a total number of 535 patients in the final EV cohort (64 IDH1 mutated and 471 IDH1 wildtype). Data splitting is summarized in Fig. 1.

div.head: Image preprocessing, feature extraction, and feature selection
div.p: All images were downloaded in the Neuroimaging Informatics Technology Initiative (NIfTI) format.

ey were already skull-stripped, co-registered and resampled to a 1 mm isotropic voxel size. e Z-score method was utilized for image intensity normalization and bin discretization was applied using a bin width of 25.

Eighteen first-order, 14 shape, and 74 texture (23 Gy Level Co-occurrence Matrix [GLCM], 16 Gy Level Run Length Matrix [GLRLM], 16 Gy Level Size Zone Matrix [GLSZM], 14 Gy Level Dependence Matrix [GLDM], and 5 Neighboring Gray Tone Difference Matrix [NGTDM]) radiomics features were extracted from each of the four MRI sequences using the PyRadiomics v3.1.0 with default values for other parameters. When combining MRI sequences, shape features were only used once because they are identical for different sequences. Detailed features are reported in Table S1.

Subsequently, we normalized the extracted features by the MinMax method, and in order to prevent overfitting, we then applied the Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator with 5-fold cross validation (LassoCV) to reduce the number of scaled initial features. Both feature normalization and feature selection steps were performed using the training cohort 1 and were then applied to HOIV, unlabeled, and EV cohorts to avoid data leakage.

div.head: Model development and validation
div.p: Due to IDH1 status imbalance, we employed the synthetic minority oversampling (SMOTE) technique [21]. We utilized 10 common ML classifiers including gradient boosting (GB), extreme GB (XGB), bagging, k-nearest neighbors (KNN), adaptive boosting (AdaBoost), logistic regression (LR), support vector machine (SVM), decision tree (DT), extra trees (ET), and random forest (RF).
We employed two main models: supervised and semisupervised. In the supervised approach, a prediction model was developed with each of the above classifiers using the oversampled training cohort 1.

e models were optimized using GridSearchCV with 5-fold CV and were evaluated on the HOIV and EV cohorts. In the semi-supervised approach, using the Grid-SearchCV with 5-fold CV, an initial classifier was trained on the oversampled training cohort 1 to predict pseudolabels for the unlabeled cohort. e features of training cohort 1 were then concatenated with the features of the unlabeled cohort. Similarly, the true outcome (IDH1 status) of training cohort 1 was concatenated with the pseudolabels of the unlabeled cohort to create a new training cohort with a larger sample size (training cohort 2). A second classifier was then trained on the training cohort 2 and was optimized using the GridSearchCV with 5-fold CV. is second model was then evaluated on the HOIV and EV cohorts. In order to compare the performance of different classifiers, all of the above classifiers were applied as initial and second classifiers through iterations. Figure 2 illustrates the study pipeline.

div.head: Performance metrics and statistical analysis
div.p: e performance of the models was evaluated using several metrics including sensitivity, specificity, precision, F1 score, area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC), and area under the curve (AUC). We applied bootstrapping with 1000 iterations to calculate 95% confidence intervals (95% CI). DeLong's test was employed to assess the significance of the differences in AUCs. e best models were selected based on the highest EV AUC [22]. To assess model calibration, we plotted calibration curves and calculated the Brier score, which quantifies the accuracy of predicted probabilities by measuring the mean squared difference between predicted and true outcomes. Model clinical utility was further evaluated using decision curve analysis (DCA), which estimates the net benefit of applying the model across a range of threshold probabilities. A p-value < 0.05 was considered the threshold for significance level. Scikit-learn version 1.2.2 in Python was used for model construction and evaluation.

div.head: Reporting guideline
div.p: e ME odological RadiomICs Score (METRICS) and CheckList for EvaluAtion of Radiomics research (CLEAR) checklists are provided in the supplementary material (additional file 2 and additional file 3, respectively).

div.head: Results
div.p: Training cohort 1, unlabeled cohort, HOIV cohort, and EV cohort contained 436, 151, 110, and 535 patients, respectively. ere was no significant difference in IDH1 status between the training cohort 1 and the EV cohort (p = 0.052). Patient characteristics of each cohort are shown in Table 1.

e LassoCV feature selection method yielded 17 to 46 features across different sequence combinations. We did not employ additional feature selection methods, as the number of final features in almost all models adhered to the commonly applied rule of thumb (having at least 10 observations per selected feature) [23,24]. e absence of a notable difference between training and validation Fig. 2 Study pipeline illustrating the implemented steps performance further indicated the lack of overfitting. e selected features for the best supervised and semi-supervised models are summarized in Table 2.

Overall, the best model was a semi-supervised model based on T1CE sequence with ET as the initial classifier and SVC as the final classifier. is model yielded AUCs of 0.891 and 0.951 in the HOIV cohort and EV cohort, respectively. e best supervised model was constructed with the combination of two sequences (FLAIR and T1CE) using ET as the classifier with an HOIV AUC of 0.902 and an EV AUC of 0.917 (Fig. 3). e best semisupervised model significantly outperformed the best supervised model (p-value for DeLong's test: 0.005). Table S2 presents detailed metrics for each model and Fig. 4 shows the best EV AUC of both supervised and semi-supervised models for each classifier.

We also compared the best supervised model and the supervised model constructed using the final classifier of the best semi-supervised model with the best semisupervised model for each sequence combination. For all the combinations, the best semi-supervised model yielded higher AUCs compared to both the best supervised model and the supervised model constructed using the final classifier of the best semi-supervised model, with most of the comparisons being statistically significant. Details are shown in Table 3.

Overall, both models demonstrated acceptable agreement between predicted and observed probabilities, although deviations from the perfect calibration line were observed across some probability ranges. e best semi-supervised model showed a tendency to slightly overestimate event probabilities in the mid-range and underestimate them in the low-probability and highprobability ranges. In contrast, the best supervised model displayed slight overestimation of risk in the low-probability range and underestimation in the high-probability range. A Brier score of 0.06 for the best semi-supervised model and 0.07 for the best supervised model confirmed good overall calibration performance.

e DCA demonstrated that both the best semi-supervised and supervised models provided a consistently higher net benefit than the treat-all and treat-none strategies across the entire range of threshold probabilities, indicating robust clinical utility. Notably, the best semi-supervised model demonstrated a greater net benefit, particularly at higher threshold probabilities (Fig. 5).

div.head: Discussion
div.p: Previous investigations have shown the potential of radiomics models in predicting glioma molecular markers [25][26][27]. In this study, we developed several supervised and semi-supervised ML models to predict glioma IDH1 status using various combinations of MRI sequences. A semi-supervised model employing ET as the initial classifier and SVM as the final classifier achieved the highest AUC on the EV cohort.

is model significantly outperformed the best supervised model, which used ET. Moreover, for every sequence combination, the highest EV AUC was consistently achieved by a semi-supervised model. Our best model showed good overall calibration and clinical utility. e justification for implementing semi-supervised models is that the higher training sample size may be beneficial for model training, even if some of the observations do not have labels available [28].

e value of this approach has already been investigated in imagebased prediction models. In a study by Mehta et al., a computed tomography (CT)-based convolutional neural network (CNN) model was used for lung nodule classification, with the semi-supervised approach demonstrating a higher AUC compared to the supervised approach [29]. Similar findings were reported in a study on lung cancer overall survival prediction [30]. Another study on CT-based prediction of epidermal growth factor receptor status in lung cancer showed a 7% increase in AUC when using a semi-supervised strategy compared to the supervised model [31]. Regarding breast cancer prediction, the semi-supervised approach yielded comparable results when using only half of the training images as labeled data and the other half as unlabeled, compared to using 100% of the training images as labeled data (supervised approach) for model construction [32]. In case of glioma IDH mutation, Tupe-Waghmare developed supervised and semi-supervised deep learning models using T1CE, T2W, and FLAIR images, and demonstrated that the latter strategy boosted the prediction performance [33].

In the current study, we evaluated models built using radiomics features extracted from the commonly used MRI sequences, namely T1W, T1CE, T2W, and FLAIR, either individually or in combination. e highest AUC was achieved by a semi-supervised model constructed with 24 radiomics features. In contrast, the best-performing supervised model was a multi-sequence model utilizing 30 features.

ese findings suggest that the semi-supervised approach could not only improve predictive performance but also enhance time efficiency and streamline the workflow by reducing the number of required MRI sequences and radiomics features. By taking advantage of the semi-supervised approach, we could construct a single-sequence model that outperformed all supervised models. is could be particularly important in clinical settings where not all MRI sequences are available.

e selected radiomic features capture tumor heterogeneity, shape, and intensity patterns that might be biologically relevant to IDH mutation status in gliomas. First-order statistics including RootMeanSquared, Skewness, Minimum, and InterquartileRange characterize intensity distributions, with IDH mutated tumors often showing lower cellular density and less necrosis, leading to distinctive signal patterns [34,35]. Shape descriptors such as Sphericity and Flatness highlight differences in tumor morphology, as IDH wildtype gliomas tend to present more irregular growth compared to the more circumscribed morphology of IDH mutated gliomas [36,37]. Texture features such as ZoneEntropy, Strength, and GrayLevelNonUniformity reflect microstructural complexity and intratumoral heterogeneity, which typically have lower values in IDH mutated gliomas due to their more homogeneous tissue architecture [38]. Collectively, these features suggest that radiomics can noninvasively capture biological distinctions between IDH mutated and wildtype gliomas. In Fig. 6, we have provided sample figures for both correct and false predictions.

Our study has several strengths. We utilized heterogenous multi-center public data for model development and validation. Both the training and validation cohorts contained images from multiple centers with different acquisition settings. Additionally, we validated our models using both HOIV and EV cohorts, in both of which our best models showed high performance. We also compared the performance of different MRI sequence combinations and various classifiers to identify the best sequence-classifier combination.

ese strategies enhance the generalizability and robustness of our models. Karakas et al. developed a combined clinicalradiomics model using conventional MRI sequences [39]. e authors investigated the performance of several [40]. Both of these studies only performed internal validation. Another study reported an AUC of 0.843 in an external validation cohort [41]. Our model showed a high AUC in both training and validation cohorts without the need for incorporating clinical or diffusion/perfusion MRI features. We also acknowledge several limitations. We merged the three tumor subregions and applied a single mask, as we intended to focus on the ML methods. Future studies may further compare supervised and semi-supervised models constructed upon different tumor subregions. Moreover, we did not employ advanced MRI sequences, such as diffusion-weighted imaging or perfusionweighted imaging, as most of the public datasets we used do not have such data available. Furthermore, clinical data were not integrated into our models. However, we were able to build highly accurate models using imaging data alone. Future studies may investigate the potential value of additional clinical features.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: Taking advantage of unlabeled data, we constructed semi-supervised models and found superior performance compared to supervised models in both HOIV and EV cohorts. Notably, the best-performing semi-supervised model in our study required only a single MRI sequence, making it more time-efficient compared to the best supervised model. These findings highlight the potential of semi-supervised learning approaches in medical imaging, where labeled data might be limited. Future research should further explore the integration of semi-supervised learning into real-world workflows.
